options.optionText: A styling language that describes the presentation of HTML documents
options.explanation: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML elements look — colors, layout, fonts, spacing, and more.

options.optionText: A programming language used to build web servers
options.explanation: CSS is not a programming language and doesn't run on servers. That's the domain of Node.js, Python, etc.

options.optionText: A markup language for structuring web content
options.explanation: HTML is the markup language for structure. CSS handles presentation.

options.optionText: A database query language for web applications
options.explanation: CSS has nothing to do with databases. SQL is the query language for relational databases.

question: What is the difference between classes and IDs in CSS?

options.optionText: IDs are unique per page and have higher specificity; classes can be reused on multiple elements
options.explanation: An ID (#) must be unique in the document and has specificity of (0,1,0,0). A class (.) can be applied to many elements and has specificity of (0,0,1,0).

options.optionText: Classes are unique per page; IDs can be reused on multiple elements
options.explanation: It's the other way around — IDs should be unique, classes are reusable.

options.optionText: IDs and classes have identical specificity and can both be reused
options.explanation: Their specificity differs significantly: an ID selector outweighs any number of class selectors.

options.optionText: IDs apply styles inline; classes apply styles globally
options.explanation: Both are external/internal stylesheet selectors. Inline styles use the style attribute directly on the element.

question: Explain the CSS box model and the layout components that it consists of.

options.optionText: Content, padding, border, and margin — each wrapping the previous layer outward
options.explanation: The box model defines how space is calculated: content area → padding → border → margin, from inner to outer.

options.optionText: Width, height, color, and font-size properties applied to every element
options.explanation: Those are CSS properties, not the box model layers.

options.optionText: Header, body, footer, and sidebar sections of a web page
options.explanation: Those are page layout regions, not the CSS box model.

options.optionText: Flexbox, Grid, Float, and Position layout systems in CSS
options.explanation: Those are layout mechanisms, separate from the box model concept.

question: What's the difference between a relative, fixed, absolute and statically positioned element?

options.optionText: Static is default flow; relative offsets from its normal position; absolute positions relative to nearest positioned ancestor; fixed positions relative to the viewport
options.explanation: position: static is the default. relative moves the element but keeps its space. absolute removes it from flow, anchored to a positioned ancestor. fixed anchors to the viewport and doesn't scroll.

options.optionText: All four values position elements relative to the viewport
options.explanation: Only fixed positions relative to the viewport. The others use different reference points.

options.optionText: Absolute and fixed are the same; relative and static are the same
options.explanation: They are all distinct values with different layout behavior.

options.optionText: Relative removes the element from document flow; absolute keeps it in flow
options.explanation: It's the opposite — absolute removes the element from normal document flow; relative keeps its reserved space.

question: What is a CSS preprocessor and why use one?

options.optionText: A tool that extends CSS with variables, nesting, mixins, and functions, then compiles to standard CSS
options.explanation: Preprocessors like Sass and Less add programming-like features to CSS, improving maintainability and reducing repetition. The output is plain CSS browsers can read.

options.optionText: A browser extension that applies CSS styles faster than the standard parser
options.explanation: Preprocessors are build-time tools, not runtime browser extensions.

options.optionText: A JavaScript library that adds animations to CSS properties
options.explanation: Preprocessors are not JavaScript libraries and don't add animation capabilities.

options.optionText: A minification tool that removes whitespace and comments from CSS files
options.explanation: Minification is a separate optimization step. Preprocessors add authoring features rather than reduce file size.

question: Describe pseudo-elements and discuss what they are used for.

options.optionText: Virtual elements created via CSS (::before, ::after) used to insert decorative content or style specific parts of an element
options.explanation: Pseudo-elements like ::before, ::after, ::first-line, ::first-letter target sub-parts of elements or insert generated content without extra HTML markup.

options.optionText: HTML elements that are hidden from screen readers
options.explanation: Pseudo-elements are CSS constructs, not hidden HTML elements.

options.optionText: JavaScript methods that manipulate the CSS of an element at runtime
options.explanation: Pseudo-elements are purely a CSS concept defined in stylesheets.

options.optionText: Selectors that target elements based on user interaction states like hover or focus
options.explanation: Those are pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus). Pseudo-elements (::before) are different — they create or target sub-parts rather than states.

question: Have you played around with the new CSS Flexbox or Grid specs?

options.optionText: Yes — Flexbox is one-dimensional (row or column) ideal for component layout; Grid is two-dimensional ideal for page layout
options.explanation: Flexbox handles single-axis alignment (nav bars, card rows). Grid handles two-dimensional layouts (full page grids, dashboard). They complement each other and are often used together.

options.optionText: Flexbox and Grid are identical in functionality; Grid is just the newer version
options.explanation: They solve different problems. Flexbox is one-dimensional; Grid is two-dimensional.

options.optionText: Flexbox is for vertical layouts only; Grid is for horizontal layouts only
options.explanation: Flexbox works on either axis (row or column). Grid handles both simultaneously.

options.optionText: Grid replaced Flexbox and Flexbox is now deprecated
options.explanation: Neither is deprecated. Both are modern, widely supported, and serve complementary purposes.

question: Explain CSS sprites, and how you would implement them on a page or site.

options.optionText: A single image file containing multiple images, displayed individually using background-position to reduce HTTP requests
options.explanation: CSS sprites combine icons/images into one file, then use background-image + background-position to show only the needed portion. This was crucial for performance before HTTP/2.

options.optionText: Animated CSS keyframe sequences applied to HTML elements
options.explanation: CSS animations use @keyframes. Sprites are about combining static images into one file.

options.optionText: A JavaScript library for creating sprite-based games in the browser
options.explanation: CSS sprites are a CSS technique for icon management, not a game development library.

options.optionText: SVG icons embedded directly inside HTML markup
options.explanation: Inline SVG is a different technique. Sprites use a single raster (or SVG) file with background-position offsets.

question: Describe z-index and how a stacking context is formed.

options.optionText: z-index controls the stack order of overlapping elements; a stacking context is created by positioned elements with z-index, opacity < 1, transforms, and similar properties
options.explanation: z-index only works on positioned or flex/grid items. A new stacking context is formed by position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, will-change, isolation: isolate, etc. Elements inside a context are ordered independently.

options.optionText: z-index applies to every element regardless of its position property
options.explanation: z-index only applies to positioned elements (not static) or flex/grid children.

options.optionText: A higher z-index always wins regardless of stacking contexts
options.explanation: z-index comparisons only apply within the same stacking context. A z-index of 9999 inside a low-priority context can still appear behind a z-index: 1 in a parent context.

options.optionText: Stacking context is another name for the CSS cascade
options.explanation: The cascade determines which style rule wins. Stacking context determines how elements overlap visually on the z-axis.

question: Explain the basic rules of CSS Specificity.

options.optionText: Specificity is scored as (inline, ID, class/attr/pseudo-class, element) — higher score wins when multiple rules target the same element
options.explanation: Specificity is calculated as a four-part tuple: inline styles > IDs > classes/attributes/pseudo-classes > elements/pseudo-elements. !important overrides all but is best avoided.

options.optionText: The last rule written in the stylesheet always wins regardless of selectors
options.explanation: Order matters only when specificity is equal. Higher specificity always overrides later rules with lower specificity.

options.optionText: Specificity only applies to class selectors, not IDs or elements
options.explanation: All selector types contribute to specificity.

options.optionText: Specificity is reset to zero after each CSS rule block
options.explanation: Specificity is a property of each selector, calculated per-rule — there's no reset mechanism.

question: What does * { box-sizing: border-box; } do? What are its advantages?

options.optionText: Makes padding and border included in the element's declared width/height, making layout calculations more predictable
options.explanation: With border-box, a 200px wide element stays 200px wide even after adding padding or border. Without it (content-box), padding and border add to the declared width, causing unexpected overflow.

options.optionText: Removes all default browser margins and paddings from every element
options.explanation: That's what a CSS reset does. box-sizing: border-box only changes how width/height are calculated.

options.optionText: Makes every element display as a block-level element
options.explanation: box-sizing has nothing to do with display type.

options.optionText: Adds a visible border to every element for debugging purposes
options.explanation: box-sizing: border-box doesn't add any visible borders. It changes the box model calculation.

question: What are the different ways to visually hide content (and make it available only for screen readers)?

options.optionText: Use a visually-hidden utility class with position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0,0,0,0)
options.explanation: This technique keeps content in the DOM and accessible to screen readers while hiding it visually. display: none and visibility: hidden both remove content from the accessibility tree.

options.optionText: Use display: none to hide the element from sighted users while screen readers still read it
options.explanation: display: none removes the element from both visual rendering AND the accessibility tree, so screen readers ignore it too.

options.optionText: Use opacity: 0 to make content invisible but readable by screen readers
options.explanation: opacity: 0 hides the content visually but the element is still interactive and takes up space — not ideal for screen-reader-only content.

options.optionText: Use visibility: hidden — screen readers will still announce the content
options.explanation: visibility: hidden hides the element from both sighted users and screen readers. Use the visually-hidden pattern instead.

question: Is there any reason you'd want to use translate() instead of absolute positioning?

options.optionText: Yes — translate() uses GPU compositing and doesn't trigger layout reflow, making animations smoother and more performant
options.explanation: translate() is processed on the compositor thread (with will-change or transform), avoiding expensive layout and paint steps. Absolute positioning changes geometry and triggers reflow on every frame.

options.optionText: No — absolute positioning and translate() have identical performance characteristics
options.explanation: They are very different in performance. translate() avoids layout; absolute positioning triggers it.

options.optionText: translate() is only available in CSS animations, not for static positioning
options.explanation: transform: translate() can be used statically on any element, not just inside animations.

options.optionText: absolute positioning always creates a new GPU layer; translate() does not
options.explanation: It's the other way — transform (including translate) promotes elements to their own compositing layer, which is why they're faster for animations.

question: What does Accessibility (a11y) mean in a CSS context?

options.optionText: Writing CSS that ensures sufficient color contrast, focus visibility, readable font sizes, and no content hidden from assistive technologies unintentionally
options.explanation: Accessibility in CSS means: WCAG-compliant contrast ratios, visible :focus styles, scalable units (rem/em over px), not using display: none or visibility: hidden to hide meaningful content from screen readers.

options.optionText: Using only black and white colors to ensure universal readability
options.explanation: Color is fine; what matters is sufficient contrast ratio (4.5:1 for normal text per WCAG AA).

options.optionText: Adding ARIA attributes to CSS selectors
options.explanation: ARIA attributes are HTML attributes, not CSS. CSS can style based on ARIA attributes but cannot add them.

options.optionText: Minifying CSS files so they load faster for users with slow connections
options.explanation: Performance optimization is valuable but not what a11y specifically means in a CSS context.

question: What's the difference between SCSS and Sass?

options.optionText: SCSS uses CSS-like curly brace syntax; Sass (indented syntax) uses indentation with no braces or semicolons — both compile to CSS
options.explanation: Both are syntaxes of the same Sass preprocessor. SCSS (.scss) is the more popular choice as it's a superset of CSS. Sass (.sass) uses indentation-based syntax similar to Python/YAML.

options.optionText: Sass is a newer version of SCSS with additional features
options.explanation: Neither is newer — they're two syntaxes of the same tool. SCSS was introduced later but is not 'more advanced'.

options.optionText: SCSS requires a build step; Sass runs natively in the browser
options.explanation: Both require a build step to compile to CSS. Neither runs natively in browsers.

options.optionText: SCSS is for React projects; Sass is for plain HTML projects
options.explanation: Both can be used in any project type. The choice is purely syntax preference.

question: Explain CSS Custom Properties (variables) and their advantages over preprocessor variables.

options.optionText: CSS custom properties (--name) are resolved at runtime in the browser, support cascade/inheritance, and can be changed with JavaScript — unlike Sass variables which are compiled away
options.explanation: CSS variables (--primary-color: blue) are live in the browser. They cascade, inherit, and can be updated via JS (element.style.setProperty). Sass variables are static — compiled out before the browser sees them.

options.optionText: CSS custom properties and Sass variables are functionally identical at runtime
options.explanation: Sass variables don't exist at runtime — they're compiled to static values. CSS custom properties are dynamic browser values.

options.optionText: CSS custom properties are only available in CSS Grid and Flexbox contexts
options.explanation: CSS custom properties work everywhere in CSS — they're not limited to any layout system.

options.optionText: CSS custom properties must be declared in the :root selector and cannot be scoped to components
options.explanation: :root is common for global variables, but custom properties can be scoped to any selector and will inherit to child elements.
